title: Indian Gallerist Sundaram Tagore Credits Friendships for His International Success
summary: “Art is wealth we must share,” said Sundaram Tagore. “And that has been my mission for the last 25 years: to find artists and share them with the world.” Tagore founded the eponymous Sundaram Tagore Gallery in 2000. It now has spaces in New York, Singapore, and, most recently, London. But his career has always extended beyond the gallery: He is a writer, scholar, collector, filmmaker, and above all, a friend to art and artists. “I don’t follow the market,” he added. “I follow instinct. And friendships.” His faith in friendship—and in art as something carried between people—began long before he opened a gallery. Born in 1961 into one of India’s most culturally influential families, Tagore grew up around Jorasanko Thakur Bari, the family’s ancestral home in Kolkata, eastern India, before moving between the towns of Santiniketan and Delhi. Jorasanko was also the birthplace of his great-granduncle Rabindranath Tagore , the poet, educator, and painter who, in 1913, became the first Asian and first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. “Kolkata, once the capital of British India, was exceptionally cosmopolitan,” Tagore recalled. “Not many people know that the first Bauhaus exhibition outside Europe was staged in the city in 1922, with works by Paul Klee and Wassily Kandinsky shown alongside leading modern Indian artists .” His childhood home drew a steady procession of intellectuals, political activists, and cultural leaders. His father, Subho Tagore, was part of that world. “He was a poet, a painter, and a rebel of a kind,” Tagore said. In 1943, Subho helped form the Calcutta Group, an early modernist art collective that rejected Romanticism in favor of a more urgent, socially engaged visual language. Its artists sold work to raise funds amid World War II, India’s independence movement, and the Bengal famine of 1943—a catastrophe, exacerbated by British colonial policies, that killed millions. “There was always an understanding that whatever resources you possessed, whether money, education, influence, or knowledge, you had a responsibility to use them in the service of others,” Tagore noted. The lesson stayed with him. Drawn to art from an early age, Tagore studied in the United States before pursuing doctoral research at Oxford University on how modernism traveled between cultures. “Unlike European modernism , Indian modernism did not reject tradition. We went back to it,” he said. “We didn’t reject figuration for abstraction; we embraced it.” Indian modernists including Amrita Sher-Gil , M.F. Husain , S.H. Raza , and F.N. Souza absorbed international styles and movements while remaining rooted in their own histories. “We found a synthesis,” he added. “That has been our greatest civilizational strength.” Yet when he moved to New York in the ’90s, working on exhibitions and later joining Pace Gallery , Tagore became increasingly aware that modern and contemporary art in the West was still presented as a largely European and American story dominated by white men. He opened his own gallery on Greene Street in SoHo as an experiment in synthesis—a place where artists across countries, movements, and generations could be brought into conversation. Early exhibitions championed Indian-born artists and Minimalists including Sohan Qadri and Natvar Bhavsar alongside overlooked women of the New York School , such as Susan Weil , Merrill Wagner , and Joan Vennum . Tagore formed close friendships with artists, gaining a deeper understanding of their work. By sharing that understanding, he helped them claim space in art historical conversations on their own terms. Weil, for example, was often known primarily as Robert Rauschenberg ’s wife, but she herself was a master of mixed-media painting. “She had an extraordinary ability to make time visible, to hold movement, memory, and the passage of a single moment within one composition,” he said. The same instinct led him to show works by Japanese artist Hiroshi Senju after encountering his monumental waterfall paintings at the Japan pavilion at the 1995 Venice Biennale. He later added Pakistani American artist Anila Quayyum Agha , known for elaborately patterned steel cubes that transform entire rooms through shadow and light, and American painter Judith Murray , whose large, colorful abstractions combine raw energy with a sense of the sublime. The gallery was already internationalizing the New York art world, carrying forward the cross-cultural curiosity and adventurous spirit of Tagore’s childhood home. “I was interested in artists who expanded my understanding of the universe,” Tagore said. After several years in SoHo, the gallery moved to its current Chelsea home on West 26th Street. Tagore opened a Hong Kong outpost in 2007, which ran until 2020, followed in 2012 by a space at Singapore’s Gillman Barracks, where it became the district’s first New York gallery. A permanent London presence followed, and a new space in the upscale district of St. James’s opened earlier this year. The gallery’s expansion coincided with the rapid globalization of the art market. “I showed at art fair after art fair. It was the most democratic way to understand which artists and ideas audiences and collectors resonated with,” he said. From Art SG , Kiaf SEOUL , Zona Maco , and EXPO Chicago to Art Mumbai and Abu Dhabi Art , Tagore built relationships with an increasingly nomadic collecting community moving across the global cultural calendar. Only around 10 percent of his collectors, he said, are Indian. The rest are spread across the United States, the United Kingdom, Asia, and the Middle East. But that globalization, particularly from the 2010s onward, brought its own excesses. “There was a time when New York galleries stayed open until midnight on Thursdays, Fridays, and Saturdays, or when the street outside a Jasper Johns exhibition would be packed,” Tagore said. He remembers an art world in which artists, gallerists, and collectors “experimented more,” and gallery-going was part of the city’s social and intellectual life. “It’s a lot more commercialized now,” he said, adding, “including friendships.” Still, Tagore remains rooted in the values that brought him this far. Beyond exhibitions, the gallery hosts poetry readings, films, musical performances, book launches, and conversations, programmed “not to please, but to connect with purpose.”

title: BBC launches art-dealing TV competition series featuring Artsy.
summary: U.K. TV channel BBC Two will premiere a new six-episode competition series centered on art dealing this week. Titled The Big Deal with Steph McGovern , the show will air on Thursday, August 13th. The premise pits 14 contestants with little to no art-market experience against one another as they try to turn a profit dealing contemporary art. Presented by broadcaster Steph McGovern, the series airs at 8 pm on BBC Two and the streaming platform iPlayer, with an earlier premiere on BBC Northern Ireland on August 12. Artsy features prominently in the fourth episode, in which contestants source artworks from two emerging artists in Berlin—Argentine painter Celeste Najt and duo 44flavours —and sell them via an Artsy Auction . Artsy vice president of marketing Ani Petrov is a judge on the episode. The Artsy auction is one of six real-world sales challenges contestants face in the series. Other episodes send contestants to auction off work by Royal College of Art graduates, furnish two luxury homes to a client brief, and sell prints and limited editions in Margate alongside artist Margo McDaid . They are also tasked with curating a collection for the cabaret bar aboard the cruise ship Queen Anne, pitching a high-end sculpture to industry insiders at Frieze London , and selling at the Affordable Art Fair . The winning pair will take home some £50,000 ($67,520) worth of art. Other judges throughout the series judging contestants’ efforts are series expert Cordelia de Freitas, alongside guest specialists including gallerist and curator Matt Carey-Williams, McDaid, and Petrov. McGovern, a business journalist known for hosting daytime talk show Steph’s Packed Lunch and news program BBC Breakfast , has described the format as “ The Apprentice for the art world, but the deals are all real, and it’s as much about the hustle as it is about art.” She has a personal connection to the subject: her father is an artist and a graduate of the Royal College of Art. “My dad was the first person I called when I got this job,” she said. BBC Arts head Suzy Klein said the series aims to “pull back the curtain” on the art market, offering “a fresh insight into how art is discovered, bought, and sold.” The show is produced by Stellify Media, the Belfast-based company behind the project since it was first announced under the working title The Art Game at the 2023 Belfast Media Festival. It was co-commissioned by BBC Arts and BBC Northern Ireland as part of the Hot House initiative, with support from Northern Ireland Screen.

title: Uffizi Galleries in Florence announce $57 million transformation.
summary: Florence’s Uffizi Galleries have announced a two-year, €50 million (roughly $57 million) transformation of the Uffizi Gallery, Palazzo Pitti, and Boboli Gardens, which the institution has described as an operation “without precedent” in scope. Uffizi director Simone Verde unveiled the plans this week, saying the roughly 40 individual projects will allow the museum to “present an even better image to the world than it does today,” according to a statement reported by The Art Newspaper . Rather than closing the museum, the work will proceed in stages so visitors can continue to see the storied collection throughout construction. With the revamp, the Uffizi is rethinking how it presents its holdings, and galleries are being reorganized chronologically and geographically. The museum’s star attractions will also receive more devoted space. The museum has already offered a preview of that approach with its redesigned rooms devoted to Sandro Botticelli , where The Birth of Venus (1486) and La Primavera (1477) now face each other in new hermetically sealed cases meant to improve both conservation and viewing conditions. Other planned work includes a new introductory exhibition space on the history of the collection at the Uffizi, budgeted at €2.4 million ($2.8 million), along with a lighting overhaul in the Palatine Gallery and new air-handling systems and accessibility upgrades across the complex. At Palazzo Pitti, the largely unused “Piano degli Occhi,” a 1,000-square-meter space on the palace’s top floor, will be converted into new exhibition galleries for €4.9 million ($5.7 million). In the Boboli Gardens, the 17th-century “amphitheatre” and the Fountain of Neptune will undergo a €3 million ($3.5 million) restoration. Half of the budget will come from ticket sales, and half from the Italian government’s culture ministry, The Art Newspaper reported, with the various projects initiated or planned since Verde took over the Uffizi’s administration in 2024. Additional elements have already been completed include the restoration of the Flemish Masters rooms, which reopened in July 2024. A spokesperson for Verde told the publication that finished projects were included in the announcement “out of a sense of seriousness, to avoid triumphalist communications before concrete results had been achieved.” The transformation follows other recent changes across the complex. These include a new entrance at Palazzo Pitti that opened in July and the reopening of the Vasari Corridor, the elevated Medici passageway connecting the Uffizi to the Pitti across the Ponte Vecchio bridge, after an eight-year restoration completed in December 2024. The Uffizi separately announced a €50 million ($57 million), eight-year masterplan for the Boboli Gardens in 2022, focused on climate resilience and accessibility, distinct from this new initiative. The investment underscores the challenge facing one of the world’s most visited museums: preserving centuries-old architecture and masterworks by Botticelli, Leonardo da Vinci , Michelangelo , Raphael , Titian , and Caravaggio while accommodating millions of visitors each year.

title: Our Favorite Artworks under $2,500 at Foundations
summary: Every art collection starts with one work—and Foundations 2026 , Artsy’s annual showcase of emerging art, is the perfect place to start. Here, you’ll find original paintings, photography, sculpture, and prints by more than 240 rising artists at over 85 galleries worldwide, all priced to put a first artwork—or a new addition to a growing collection—within reach. Buying your first piece doesn’t need to be complicated. It can be as simple as finding a piece that stops you: a color that matches a memory, a subject that makes you laugh, a texture you want to live with. After all, art is, and should be, intensely personal. Here, our team has combed Foundations for the works under $2,500 we can’t stop thinking about. Under $1,000 Vanessa McKernan Embrace , 2025 Presented by Abbozzo Gallery Price: $850 Embrace, 2025 Vanessa McKernan Abbozzo Gallery If I’ve learned one thing in this life, it’s that there’s nothing better than a hug when things get tough. This exquisitely colored painting by Canadian painter Vanessa McKernan captures an embrace that fully conveys why they can be so transporting. Resting in each other’s arms, the two central faces—parent and child, perhaps—have their eyes closed, their expressions intimate and peaceful. Between the expressionist figures in the center and the floating orange flowers, I find the whole scene immensely calming: something from a dream in which everything works out okay in the end. McKernan is based in the Ottawa Valley countryside, where she says the surrounding nature influences her work. Personally, I can see the influence of Pierre Bonnard in her color choices, as well as in the abstract gestures toward greenery in the background. —Josie Thaddeus-Johns, associate director of content Under $2,000 Maremi Andreozzi Genevieve Estelle Jones , 2026 Presented by Adah Rose Gallery Price: $1,200 Genevieve Estelle Jones, 2026 Maremi Andreozzi Adah Rose Gallery Featureless silhouettes are the subjects of Maremi Andreozzi ’s series “A Life Well Lived.” Genevieve Estelle Jones (2026) is one such protagonist. Even though the painting’s face doesn’t have eyes to catch yours, you can still feel her stare. I quickly discovered that Jones was an amateur woman naturalist in the 1800s, often called “the other Audubon,” referring to the famed American conservationist. Andreozzi lifted details from existing portraits of Jones—the perfect collar, the dangling earrings—and dropped them into this surreal portrait. The silhouette is surrounded by symbols of what Jones was all about: crisscrossing twigs and delicate bird eggs accompany her silhouette, a nod to her overlooked legacy. I chose this work because I love all things Victorian, and Genevieve Estelle Jones is a reminder that there’s always a surprising figure or fact (the more obscure the better) that can light up my day. —Sydney Gelman, copywriter Maja Sisse Trout Circle , 2024 Presented by Galleri Zeuthen Price: $1,750 Trout Circle, 2024 Maja Sisse Galleri Zeuthen I’ve always had a soft spot for sculptures that play with our sense of perception. That’s why I was immediately drawn to Trout Circle (2024) by Danish artist Maja Sisse , on view in Galleri Zeuthen ’s Foundations presentation . Three ceramic trout chase one another nose-to-tail, forming a near-perfect ring, enmeshed in what could be a synchronized swimming routine. Their wide, glassy eyes and slightly gawky expressions make the whole arrangement feel as though they might break formation at any moment. What I love most is Sisse’s handling of the ceramic surface. Mottled blues, greens, creams, and rusty browns give the fish the weathered look of something dredged from the bottom of a river, while the carefully rendered scales and fins give each one a wonderfully tactile presence. Caught in this circle, these trout seem destined to keep following one another forever. It’s the kind of sculpture I’d happily let swim circles on my shelf. —Arun Kakar, senior art market editor Under $2,500 House of Goblin Yon Oak , 2025 Presented by Cob Price: £1,500 Yon Oak, 2025 House of Goblin Cob I was drawn to this perfect ceramic sconce, an outlier among the works in Foundations, for the way it marries form and function. Shaped like an oak leaf with fluid, biomorphic lines—reminiscent of 20th-century artist Jean (a.k.a. Hans) Arp —it feels timeless and a little strange, spare yet whimsical. I’ve only just learned about House of Goblin , the English artist collective behind it, whose hand-built ceramics merge utilitarian and sculptural approaches. They source many of their glaze materials from natural sites across the U.K.; here, glazes interact, as a matte, mossy green gives way to a bubbly texture, like a pale minty foam. The title adds another layer of charm: Yon Oak references Alfred Tennyson’s 1889 poem “The Oak,” which follows a tree through the seasons as a metaphor for aging and the strength we gain over time. It’s a lot for one small object—and still, it’s a lovely perch for a candle. —Casey Lesser, director of editorial and content Polina Osipova Arrow from archives , 2025 Presented by JO-HS Price: $2,500 Arrow from archives, 2025 Polina Osipova JO-HS I first learned of Polina Osipova from a video of the artist operating Pearl Mechanism 2 (2020), a whimsical contraption she’d made with strings of pearls. The video was mesmerizing, delightful, and the perfect introduction to her nontraditional practice. Born in Russia, Osipova now lives and works in London, and she had a solo exhibition, “ A Living Inheritance ,” with JO-HS in New York earlier this year. Osipova comes from a Chuvash family, a Turkic ethnic group with a long, complex history in Russia and Central Asia, whose culture and language were shaped by Mongolian, Arabic, and Persian influences. Arrow From the Archives (2025) is emblematic of her most recent works and based on this heritage. Here, the artist transforms imagery from family photographs into childlike objects. She uses embroidery and needlework from Chuvash traditions as a way of stitching her ancestral knowledge into these works. I particularly like Arrow From the Archives because its plush softness is counterbalanced by the sharp point of the arrow. The bow and arrow are objects of childhood imagination, as well as of protection. —Katie White, senior staff writer

title: 5 Artists on Our Radar in August 2026
summary: No hay sol en el Verano, 2026 Almo Talud Eric Firestone Gallery Summer Bloom, 2026 Alex Maceda Half Gallery “Artists on Our Radar” is a monthly series focused on five artists who have our attention. Utilizing our art expertise and Artsy data, we’ve determined which artists made an impact this past month through new gallery representation, exhibitions, auctions, art fairs, or fresh works on Artsy. Alex Maceda B. 1989, San Francisco Bay Area. Lives and works in New York City. Downward Dog, 2026 Alex Maceda Half Gallery Artist Alex Maceda draws from her Filipina heritage and devout Catholic upbringing in her small-scale biomorphic paintings. The artist has likened these works to domestic shrines or altars, intended for meditative purposes. Now in “ Sun Salutations ,” the artist’s first solo exhibition with Half Gallery , on view through August 13th, Maceda takes inspiration from transcendental women artists such as Hilma af Klint and Agnes Pelton who pursued spiritual dimensions through artmaking. Maceda lived and worked for a time in California’s Joshua Tree, finding, like many other artists before her, serenity in the solitude of the desert. In “Sun Salutations” the sunburnt colors of that landscape are on full display in 10 joyful paintings rendered in the dawn-like hues of yellows, pinks, and reds. The show’s title refers to the yoga sequence of poses traditionally performed at sunrise, synchronizing the breath with movements to awaken the body and build internal heat. She seeks a similar rhythmic alignment through her artworks. Maceda holds an MFA in painting from the New York Studio School (2026), an MBA from Stanford Graduate School of Business (2018), and a BA in classical studies from Dartmouth College (2011). She has had solo exhibitions at Herron House (2024); Dorado 806 Projects (2024); Upper Market Gallery (2024); and 29 Palms Art Gallery (2023). This year, her works have been featured in the group show “Austin Friends Fair” at Half Gallery and “Disappearing Boundaries” at Harper’s . Almo Talud B. 1985, Miami. Lives and works in Medellin, Colombia. Viaje al Guamo, 2026 Almo Talud Eric Firestone Gallery Artist Almo Talud paints folkloric scenes that consider Latino identity through a queer lens, offering masculinity, memory, and fantasy. The artist was born in Miami, but grew up in the small city of Manizales, Colombia. His paintings depict men in celebratory moments, dressed in colorful attire and surrounded by horses. The images draw from his childhood memories, but challenge dominant patriarchal culture that surrounded him through his use of soft hues and thin lyrical marks of acrylic paint and pastel. “I approach memory as a living material, imprecise, mutable, and charged with affection,” the artist has said . “Within this process, error, distortion, and formal synthesis become essential tools for revealing deeper layers of identity.” Talud completed his secondary education in Bogotá, and then moved to New York, where he studied at the Art Students League of New York for four years. His works are inspired by self-taught artists, such as the Colombian artist Noé Léon . Talud’s work was recently on view in the group exhibition “ General Assembly ” at Eric Firestone Gallery and was also presented by the gallery in a two-artist installation with ceramics by Torben Gammelgaard at NOMAD Hamptons 2026 . Tony Dongfang Zhao B. 2002, Beijing, China. Lives and works in New York. Tower, 2026 Tony Dongfang Zhao C24 Gallery Drive My Car, 2025 Tony Dongfang Zhao C24 Gallery New York–based artist Tony Zhao paints vignettes of daily life, cropped to focus on minute details—empty seats on a train, a bracelet around a wrist, a light fixture. These seemingly mundane scenes take on a filmic quality in his oil on canvas compositions, thanks to his considered framing and his constrained, brooding color palette. Currently, his work is on view in the two-artist exhibition “ Contact Points ” at New York’s C24 Gallery through September 4th. Born and raised in Beijing, Zhao received his BFA from the Rhode Island School of Design in 2024. Before that, he worked as an independent curator and educator at UCCA Center for Contemporary Art in Beijing, where a group exhibition of his own work was held in 2020. He also had a solo exhibition, “Lake House,” at A/W Space in London in 2024, and has been included in group shows at Union Street Gallery in Chicago and Gelman Gallery in Providence. Heidi Howard B. 1986, New York City. Lives and works in New York City. Self- Rauschenberg Pink Periwinkle, 2026 Heidi Howard David B. Smith Gallery Bonnard Redon Bouquet, 2026 Heidi Howard David B. Smith Gallery New York artist Heidi Howard grew up surrounded by creativity as the daughter of avant-garde composer Earl Howard and installation artist Liz Phillips , shaping the way she approaches artmaking. Known for her still lifes, en plein air landscapes, and particularly her portraits, Howard sees art as inextricably tied to daily life. Before painting a portrait, Howard typically gets to know her model for months or even years, developing an understanding of their personality and aesthetics. She most often paints these portraits in person, in her home, even cooking meals for her models after the session is finished. Her paintings are characterized by their Dayglo palette, dancelike brush strokes, and embrace of irresolution. In recent years, Howard’s practice has expanded beyond the confines of the canvas to include site-specific wall paintings, indoor and outdoor sculpture. Her work is currently on view in “ Pistil Forms ,” a duo exhibition with Esteban Cabeza de Baca at David B. Smith Gallery , the pair’s second collaboration at the gallery, following 2024’s “Night & Day Dreams.” Howard has also exhibited at Wave Hill Garden and Cultural Center, the Queens Museum , the Hunterdon Museum of Art, James Cohan Gallery, and Gaa Gallery , and has held residencies including the Terra Summer Residency, the Rauschenberg Residency, Carrizozo AIR, and Palazzo Monti . Her first monograph, Colors make us do vibrant deeds! , launched in 2024. Michael Bühler-Rose B. 1980, New Brunswick, New Jersey. Lives and works between New York City and Mysore, India. Lichtenstein Brushtroke (Flowers), 2025 Michael Bühler-Rose New Discretions USM, Summer '26 (01), 2026 Michael Bühler-Rose Halsey McKay Gallery Artist Michael Bühler-Rose brings the Renaissance technique of wood intarsia and inlay to contemporary art, using the intricate medium to create deeply personal works that memorialize individual collections such as stacks of books, ritual paraphernalia, and print boxes. Since his teenage years, Bühler-Rose practiced Vaishnavism, a branch of Hinduism devoted to the god Vishnu, and has devoted himself to the study of Sanskrit. Simultaneously, he was involved in the punk and hardcore music scenes in the Northeast. At 17, Bühler-Rose first traveled to India, becoming a Hare Krishna, renouncing his earthly possessions. Now, 25 years later, living as a layperson, the artist’s works reflect upon the value of objects in our lives and their role in ritual, image worship, religious practice and as art objects. As he told Another Magazine , his work draws “parallels between the artist as priest, art object as a deity, the gallery as a post-Enlightenment temple, and the installation of the artwork as a ritual.” Right now, Bühler-Rose’s work is currently on view in “ Halo in a Haystack ,” at Halsey McKay Gallery in Easthampton, his first solo exhibition with the gallery. These works are inspired by the Studiolo of the Ducal Palace in Gubbio (1478-82), a wooden study, intended for meditation and study, now in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art . The studio is filled with illusionistic books, instruments, armor, and curiosities rendered through the art of the inlay technique intarsia. In the show, the artist focuses on one of his long-ago forfeited possessions: a copy of Halo in a Haystack , the debut LP by the New England hardcore band Converge, which has now become a sought-after collectors item. Bühler-Rose’s work has been gaining new attention of late. Earlier this year, he presented a solo booth with Brussels’s Stems Gallery at Independent Art Fair . In 2024, he opened the solo exhibition “ I Want Your Skull ,” with New Discretions . His works have also been featured at NADA Miami 2025 , NADA Miami 2023 , NADA Miami 2022 , and Future Fair 2022 with that gallery.

title: Yoshitomo Nara to present two-gallery New York exhibition at David Zwirner in October 2026.
summary: David Zwirner has announced a solo exhibition of works by Japanese artist Yoshitomo Nara , spanning the gallery’s two Chelsea locations at 537 West 20th Street and 533 West 19th Street in New York. Opening in October 2026, the show will be Nara’s first solo presentation with David Zwirner since it took on representation of the artist last November and his first major solo exhibition in New York in nearly a decade. The exhibition brings together new paintings and drawings, recent sculptures, and early works selected by the artist, tracing four decades of the artist’s practice. His childhood encounters with nature, folklore, and children’s stories in rural northern Japan, alongside a self-built radio that introduced him to popular music, have shaped a visual language he has developed since the mid-1980s. His signature figures, rendered with large heads and wide eyes, were recognized in the 1990s as carriers of raw emotion with the spirit of punk music. Over time they have become cultural touchstones, functioning for many viewers as mirrors of their own vulnerabilities. New paintings at the gallery’s 20th Street location demonstrate a significant development in Nara’s color palette, with more muted, nuanced tones and increasingly diffuse brushwork. A second group of works introduces a new technique for the artist: figures sketched in colored pencil, then developed with washes of translucent acrylic. Large-format monochrome drawings made with industrial oil-based paint sticks, meanwhile, show the range of his two-dimensional practice. Early works from the 1980s, also featured in the show, will provide a historical counterpoint. At Zwirner’s 19th Street location, 13 bronze heads from 2024—enlarged 10 times from palm-sized clay prototypes—will be on view. Coated in white urethane paint, the monumental sculptures recall the snow “monsters” of Nara’s childhood winters. Nara has seen a string of major museum shows over his career. Most recently, a major solo exhibition of the artist was shown at the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao , Spain, as well as Museum Frieder Burda, Baden-Baden, Germany, and the Hayward Gallery , London.

title: Ms. Lauryn Hill has curated a new commission by Lauren Halsey on London’s Piccadilly Lights.
summary: Rapper and singer-songwriter Ms. Lauryn Hill has curated a new site-specific commission by Los Angeles artist Lauren Halsey for Piccadilly Lights, the digital billboard overlooking London’s Piccadilly Circus, timed to the U.K. debut of Hill’s Diaspora Calling! music and arts festival. The commission, a short animated film drawing on the imagery and symbols of the global African diaspora, played on the screen on the night of August 5th for a one-night-only presentation, ahead of the festival. The project was realized in close dialogue with London-based curator Lisa Anderson. Hill and her former Fugees bandmate Wyclef Jean stood in the circus surrounded by fans. “The crowd was captivated,” Hill told the Associated Press. Jean called the moment “surreal.” The unveiling comes as Diaspora Calling! marks its 10th anniversary and travels outside the U.S. for the first time. Hill launched the festival in April 2016 at Brooklyn's Kings Theatre, opening with a gallery co-curated with MoCADA, Nader Haitian Art, and the Haiti Cultural Exchange, and a concert featuring Machel Montano, Stephen “Ragga” Marley, and Mr. Eazi, among others. She has described the project as a way of foregrounding “a resounding collective voice” across the African diaspora rather than a single narrative. The anniversary performance will take place Friday, August 7th, at the National Bowl in Milton Keynes, hosted by Dave Chappelle, with Hill and Jean performing the Fugees’ “The Score” in full for its 30th anniversary, alongside sets from Erykah Badu, YG Marley, Zion Marley, Giggs, and Fireboy DML. For Halsey, the Piccadilly Lights commission extends a run of major public projects. Her monumental sculpture park “sister dreamer, ” presented by the Los Angeles Nomadic Division (LAND) and curated by Christine Y. Kim, has been on view in South Central Los Angeles since March, with support from the Mellon Foundation and backers including LeBron James, Brad Pitt, and Larry Gagosian , whose namesake gallery represents Halsey. In 2023, she realized a rooftop commission for the Metropolitan Museum of Art , and in 2024 she presented work as part of the 60th Biennale di Venezia . Halsey has also had solo exhibitions at the Serpentine in London (2024), the Seattle Art Museum (2022), the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (2021), and the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris (2019).In 2020, she founded the Summaeverythang Community Center, which distributes free produce in South Central Los Angeles. Following Friday’s concert, Diaspora Calling! is expected to continue expanding internationally; Hill told the AP she hopes to stage further editions.

title: Meet the Gallerist Bringing World-Renowned Artists to a Tiny Greek Island
summary: On a rocky outcrop on the small Greek island of Antiparos, a waist-high bronze statue of a rabbit sits on the edge of a turquoise infinity pool. Wearing a large, tented skirt, it faces the windswept Aegean Sea from the terrace of a private home. The scene could be from a Greek dream right out of the Odyssey ; except the artwork, inspired by Japanese animism, is by renowned artist Leiko Ikemura . Good Rabbit (2018–24) is one of several works by major international artists gathered in this remote Cycladic setting for “ Melting Beauty ,” a summer exhibition organized by Thea Montauti d’Harcourt Lyginos, founder of Geneva gallery L’Appartement . The surprisingly remote location of Antiparos, Greece, is a nod to her Greek husband and years of family summers on the island. Like her gallery in Geneva, the choice of location doubles down on Montauti d’Harcourt Lyginos’s philosophy of using residential spaces for art exhibitions. Placing art in a domestic setting Inside the house, a patchwork seascape by Sean Scully hangs opposite a 5-meter-long mural by Amy Sillman . A gigantic raw-canvas triptych by Martha Jungwirth occupies the living room; paintings by younger artists appear in the kitchen and bedrooms. Right next to the archaeological site of Despotiko, the house is in an out-of-the-way spot for a show of such high-profile names; others include Yinka Shonibare , Joan Snyder , Kennedy Yanko , and Liliane Tomasko under the fluid theme dreamed up by curator Craig Burnett. Destination art shows are hardly new in the art world. Mega-gallery Hauser & Wirth has a permanent space in Menorca, Spain, for instance, while DESTE Foundation, an art organization run by Greek collector Dakis Joannou, has staged projects on nearby Hydra for well over a decade. More recently, galleries have become increasingly interested in meeting collectors where they are vacationing, whether at new art fairs in Ibiza and Saint-Tropez, or through pop-ups like this one, which runs through August 31st. During the exhibition’s opening days, the gallery directors, artists, and collectors dropping in suggested that its approach was working. Everyone, it seems, wants to be part of the dreamy Greek island lifestyle, including artists. Snyder, the acclaimed American painter, for instance, created one of her “Pond” works specifically for the show, drawn in by Burnett, with whom she’s worked for years. “It sounded intriguing to be in a show in Greece that [Burnett] was curating,” she said. “Of course I said yes.” Artworks on the theme of “Melting Beauty” Deep Pond, 2026 Joan Snyder L'Appartement Deep Pond (2026) is a muddy taupe square with a sticky acrylic void at its center. It’s dotted with tiny collaged green and pink blobs. For curator Burnett, it encapsulates the concept of “Melting Beauty.” Throughout the show, he explained, he chose works that seem in the middle of disintegration to evoke the sensual qualities that are so present in the Greek landscape beyond the residence’s borders. “It really suits the setting in terms of the title of the show—in terms of melting, the sense of liquefaction, but also the sense of the sensuality of emotion,” he said. Alongside the renowned names are several rising artists. A painting of flowy female figures by Konstantina Krikzoni fills the kitchen while Amorelle Jacox ’s gauzy symbolist canvases hang in the master bedroom. “The show is invested with this kind of feeling of eros,” Burnett said, pointing to a copy of Schiller’s On the Aesthetic Education of Man . In the book, Schiller contrasts “melting” beauty, which relaxes our minds, with the taut, rigid kind, which energizes us. A small, tabletop sculpture by Kennedy Yanko , made using her signature paint-skin and metal technique, offers a case in point. Its pink, folded form slumps sensually on its plinth, unexpectedly elegant. L’Appartement’s first off-site The island project makes more sense in light of Montauti d’Harcourt Lyginos’s career. She began at Sotheby’s in London, before moving to Geneva to work for Gagosian . When she established her own gallery in the Swiss lakeside city in 2024, she set out to create the kind of space she'd always wanted to visit: somewhere welcoming, with the feel of an apartment. “I never envisioned this sort of multinational white cube, with many spaces around the world,” she said. “That was never the ambition.” Instead, she wanted a place where visitors could sit down and talk—something she felt Geneva lacked. On Antiparos, she’s translated that vision into a real home. But why this specific island home? For Montauti d’Harcourt Lyginos, that connection starts with her name. “Thea” means goddess in Greek—a name her mother gave her, inspired by her love of ancient Greece. Then she married a Greek man, and the tie deepened. For the past decade, the family has spent its summers around the Aegean: Antiparos and nearby Paros as well as Schinoussa. “It’s really my second home,” she said. When the opportunity arose to stage an exhibition in a newly built private residence on Antiparos, she didn’t hesitate. The island, she noted, already had the right audience. “Historically, Antiparos always brought a very artsy crowd,” she said, adding that major gallerists Eva Presenhuber and Dominique Lévy both have connections to the island. It’s a haunt for Hollywood names, too: Tom Hanks and Sofia Coppola both vacation there. But the gallerist isn’t sticking around beyond summer. Montauti d’Harcourt Lyginos is already considering another off-site project, this time in Turin, Italy. “I’m 100 percent Italian,” she said with a grin. But that will be at least two years before that happens. Wall Sky Blue Grey, 2026 Sean Scully L'Appartement Flirt, 2024 Arlene Shechet L'Appartement Her first off-site exhibition taught her that such projects require more time than expected—most importantly to allow artists to create new commissions. The gallery may have escaped the white cube, but it has not escaped the logistical challenges of mounting an international exhibition. After all, “Beautiful things are difficult, right?” she said, smiling.

title: Ethiopian Painter and Artsy Vanguard alum Tesfaye Urgessa joins White Cube.
summary: White Cube has announced representation of Ethiopian painter and Artsy Vanguard alum Tesfaye Urgessa . The gallery will present his work at Frieze Seoul 2026 , where his painting Fiber of grace (Schutz) 2 (2025) will be on view, ahead of his debut solo exhibition at White Cube Hong Kong, opening September 9, 2026. Urgessa lives and works between Addis Ababa and Nürtingen, Germany, and was the first artist to represent Ethiopia in its inaugural national pavilion at the Venice Biennale in 2024 . His first solo museum presentation in Asia is currently on view at Red Brick Art Museum in Beijing, through August 9, 2026. Describing himself primarily as a draughtsman, Urgessa begins each day with drawing before turning to painting on his studio floor, working with a long brush to build densely populated compositions in which bodies appear pressed against one another, at times enmeshed with their domestic surroundings. His visual vocabulary draws on Ethiopian iconographic traditions and German Expressionism , as well as Francis Bacon and Lucian Freud , whose work he has studied closely. He attributes this breadth to a formative encounter with European art after relocating to Germany to study at the Staatliche Akademie der Bildenden Künste in Stuttgart, an experience that also brought him into contact with forms of racial and social difference new to him. Migration, familial relations, and community are recurring concerns in his work, shaped in part by his wife’s work with newly arrived migrants. In 2023, Urgessa was selected in The Artsy Vanguard , the annual selection of the most promising artists working today. “I want my figures to have almost an emotional vulnerability,” he told writer Emily Steer in an interview . The White Cube Hong Kong exhibition will bring together new paintings and works on paper made over the past year. Urgessa’s works are held in institutional collections including the Brooklyn Museum , New York; Castello di Rivoli, Turin; and the Uffizi Galleries, Florence.

title: 5 Artists to Follow at Foundations 2026
summary: Vegetable Venus, 2026 Xanthe Burdett Wilder Gallery This month on Artsy, Foundations 2026 has launched: a curated showcase highlighting artists at the beginning of their careers. With over 240 artists from around the world, this edition of Foundations is the perfect chance to discover emerging talents and buy fine art at an accessible price. At Artsy, we’ve spent the last week poring over the showcase to find our favorites. We’ve handpicked five artists whose works are worth a second look, from abstractions made of seashells and tapioca beads to cake-laden paintings of consumption. Charlene Tan B. 1982, Houston. Lives and works in San Francisco. Works available at: re.riddle Homage to Kappi (Crab), 2025 Charlene Tan re.riddle Homage to Kappi (Crab) Abalone and Rhinestones, 2025 Charlene Tan re.riddle Artist Charlene Tan was born in Houston, but she spent three years of her childhood living with her grandmother in the Philippines. There, the artist remembers visiting an indoor market in Manila and seeing stalls full of freshwater pearls, beads, and rhinestones. Now based in San Francisco, Tan’s artworks are in many ways inspired by that experience, as well as her grandmother, who was a seamstress and embroiderer. Tan creates abstract works that are inspired by tribal weaving traditions of the Philippines. Tan digitally scans found images of traditional weavings, edits them down to the essential pattern, and then retraces them by hand. The artist then adorns these patterns with pearls, iridescent shells, and Filipino food staples like ube powder or thousands of tiny pink tapioca balls. Tan has described interpreting traditional Filipino weavings as decolonizing her mindset. Tan holds a BA in history and theory of contemporary art from the San Francisco Art Institute. Her work has been shown across the U.S., including solo shows “ Warp/Weft ” at re.riddle in 2024 and “ Remembering ” at Sarah Shepard in 2023. She has also been a visiting artist at Minnesota Street Project Studios in San Francisco. Xanthe Burdett B. 1995, Devon, England. Lives and works in London. Works available at: Wilder Gallery They came upon a clearing, 2026 Xanthe Burdett Wilder Gallery Like bees, I feel them brush softly against me, 2026 Xanthe Burdett Wilder Gallery British artist Xanthe Burdett paints strange, spectral female figures that appear at once human and botanical. Painted in thin veils of green hue, these women appear translucent, even ghostly, with vines and flowers twisting through their bodies. In her painting Vegetable Venus (2026), a phantom woman reclines like an odalisque, greenery running through her body like a circulatory system. She seems to emerge from the foggy green landscape behind her. This imagery draws both from her personal memories and art historical inspirations, such as the medieval “Devonshire Hunting Tapestries” in the collection of the Victoria and Albert Museum . Burdett has described the works as concerned with “this idea of memory and history being caught in the ground and the earth beneath us—this space of the mythological animal world, but also this really fertile place that we can’t look into as humans.” Burdett graduated with an MA in painting from the Royal College of Art in 2024, after studying education, English, and drama at Cambridge. She opened a solo exhibition “ Psychopomp " at Palo Gallery in New York last fall. Her work was recently on view with Wilder Gallery at Echo Soho in London. Kriss Munsya B. 1986, Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo. Lives and works in Vancouver. Works available at: Galerie Robertson Arès Syracuse, 2022 Kriss Munsya Galerie Robertson Arès Even - Washed Out. Genetic Bomb (framed | avec encadrement), 2022 Kriss Munsya Galerie Robertson Arès Photographer and filmmaker Kriss Munsya creates vibrant, staged photographs inspired by his experiences and dreams as a Black man navigating the world. Born in Kinshasa, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Munsya moved to Belgium as a child. He was raised in Brussels and later relocated to Vancouver, where he lives and works today. As a young man, Munsya embarked on an influential hitchhiking trip from New York to Rio de Janeiro, a sojourn that became the basis of his 2015 debut feature film, Us and Them . His experiences on the road reshaped his understanding of the world, including its normalized, sometimes violent racism, and his sense of self. A self-taught artist, Munsya turned his focus to photography five years ago, coinciding with his increased involvement in social and ecological activism. His richly saturated color photographs picture Black people in gestures of intimacy and affection. He obscures his models’ faces with flowers, sequins, and fabric, anonymizing and universalizing them at once. Munsya’s work is included in the collections of Canada Council Art Bank. He was a 2021 Hopper Prize finalist and one of ArtConnect’s Artists to Watch in 2023, with work featured in The New Yorker , Vogue, and Aesthetica Magazine, among others. Olivia Sterling B. 1996, Peterborough, England. Lives and works in London. Works available at: Nibelungen Gallery Cartoon Logic, 2025 Olivia Sterling Nibelungen Gallery Are we about to Kiss?, 2024 Olivia Sterling Nibelungen Gallery British artist Olivia Sterling paints the language of consumption—one slice of cake at a time. In her paintings, hands dig into frosted, sugary cakes, devouring the confections with a frenzied intensity. Her style is informed by children’s comic books as well as satirical illustrations, and her work often hints at the politics of race and class. Sterling received her BA in fine art from the University of Derby in 2018 and her MA in painting from the Royal College of Art in 2020. That year she presented her solo show “It Clings Like a Leech” at Guts Gallery, London, and had a solo presentation, “White Bread,” at Cob in 2021. Her work has appeared in more than 50 group exhibitions in the U.K. and internationally, including at White Cube and the Saatchi Gallery. Julia Policastro B. 1992, Buffalo, New York. Lives and works in Philadelphia. Works available at: Blah Blah Gallery Lydia, 2025 Julia Policastro Blah Blah Gallery Cecily, 2025 Julia Policastro Blah Blah Gallery Artist Julia Policastro makes three-dimensional artworks that could be defined as both sculpture and painting. In these plaster, foam board, canvas, and oil works, hands emerge from pillow-like forms, holding flowers or grasping a letter between fingertips. Using a technique inspired by the 14th-century Italian quilting technique of trapunto , each of these works bears a woman’s name: Gina, Cecily, Janet. The gestures they depict are seemingly mundane, but otherworldly, reminiscent of Robert Gober ’s haunting handmade sculptures. Policastro has painted these works pale hues of whites, pinks, and yellows, giving them a faded, ghostly appearance. Her inspirations range from late medieval and early Renaissance Sienese artists to the works of Ken Price and David Hockney . Policastro received her BFA from Tyler School of Art. She has been included in group shows at Blah Blah Gallery , Deep Space Gallery , and Fleisher/Ollman, among others.

title: Daniel Arsham to create whisky-inspired performances during Frieze Seoul 2026.
summary: Artist Daniel Arsham has collaborated with Scottish distillery The Balvenie on a new whisky collection entitled “Dawn of Our Spirit,” which will be unveiled on September 1st in partnership with Frieze Seoul . The collection will be introduced through an immersive, sensorial performance directed by Arsham. The performance draws on the meditative process of turning barley grain on a malting floor, an important step in the preparation of whisky. Arsham visited the distillery’s own malting floor in Speyside, Scotland, which opened around 1931 and remains unchanged. “The distillery itself is so materially rich: the barley grain, the copper stills, the wooden casks crafted in the cooperage, combined with an array of evocative time-infused scents and ambient sounds,” Arsham said. “I’m looking forward to expressing this through our performances during Frieze Seoul .” The Balvenie’s malt master Kelsey McKechnie, who conceived the collection, called it “a true celebration of master craftmanship and the creative power of time,” adding that Arsham’s “artistic storytelling will bring the treasured and fundamental aspect of The Balvenie’s Home Malting Floor to a world stage.” The project extends Arsham’s long list of brand collaborations, which include Dior , Adidas, and Rimowa , as well as an ongoing partnership with Tiffany & Co. dating to 2021. Arsham also serves as creative director for the NBA team Cleveland Cavaliers , for whom he redesigned the team’s logo. His gallery artistic practice has continued alongside this commercial work. His most recent exhibition “ Various Thoughts ” closed at Perrotin New York in April, coinciding with the release of his autobiography, Future Relic . The Balvenie x Arsham unveiling arrives during a packed week for the Korean capital. Frieze Seoul returns to COEX in Gangnam for its fifth edition from September 2nd to 5th, hosting more than 125 galleries from 30 countries. The fair will run concurrently with Kiaf Seoul , the country’s longest-running international art fair, which will welcome 175 galleries for its 25th edition, also at the COEX. Following its Seoul debut, “Dawn of Our Spirit” will travel to New York, Shanghai, and Taipei.

title: Meet the Latvian Collector Championing a New Generation of Baltic Artists
summary: From her high-rise office overlooking Riga’s green rooftops, Vita Liberte describes the quality she looks for in art with a single word: authenticity. “You should never go after somebody,” she told Artsy. “You should think on your own, and only then you’re interesting.” That principle has guided Liberte as she and her husband, Vilnis Štrams, have assembled one of the most significant collections of contemporary Baltic art. Through VV Foundation, which they co-founded with art historian Jānis Borgs almost a decade ago, they have acquired more than 500 works, largely by artists from Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia. The collection reflects Liberte’s belief that Baltic artists are at their most compelling when they turn inward to the region’s landscapes, memories, political histories, and unresolved experiences, rather than looking westward for direction. “There is this tendency, a little bit also in Eastern European art, to look at what’s going on in the Western world,” she said. “But I always say we should do it differently.” Although the collection has grown substantially, Liberte still approaches buying as a personal process. She rarely acquires a work without first understanding the person who made it. “I need to know the artist before I buy,” she said. For Liberte, collecting is less about purchasing an object than entering a long-term relationship with an artistic practice. The artists she tracks have also changed how she sees the world. “I’ve changed as a person, also through art,” she noted. Her personal collecting journey began without extensive knowledge of contemporary art. Liberte trained as a tax lawyer, studying international law at New York University before returning to Latvia to establish her own firm. While living in New York, she became aware of the importance of private cultural patronage in the United States. “Here in Latvia, people look at art and think it’s the responsibility of the state,” she told Artsy. “When I came back, I said to myself: ‘Okay, if I like something, I can support it.’” She initially supported Latvia’s film industry, the Latvian National Symphony Orchestra, and Kim? Contemporary Art Centre, where she remains a board member. “I didn’t know much about contemporary art,” she admitted. “It’s a lot of learning for me as well.” As her collection developed, so did her education. Liberte is particularly drawn to artists who engage with the Baltic region’s Soviet and post-Soviet experience, such as Lithuanian artist Augustas Serapinas , whose work often transforms overlooked materials, spaces, and social histories. The 1990s remain an especially resonant period. For Baltic countries, the decade brought independence, instability, freedom, and economic hardship. Liberte believes artists are only now gaining enough distance to examine it fully. “The ’90s were really harsh for us, for everybody,” she said. “It’s challenging for people to go back and look at it from a good perspective, because bad and good things happened.” She sees the period as both painful and creatively fertile. Much of its material culture was lost in the desire to discard the Soviet past. “There was this thing of destroying everything,” she added. Collecting, in this context, becomes a form of preservation. In October 2026, VV Foundation will publish its first collection book with Milan-based publisher Skira. It will bring together approximately 40 works by around 30 Baltic artists, pairing each with a writer or curator to create what Liberte calls “a dialogue between artist and author.” The publication will include only a fraction of the collection, but it will articulate its commitment to documenting Baltic artistic practices while they are still developing. Liberte points to a generation of artists who have already begun receiving wider recognition. They include Lina Lapelytė , co-creator of the Golden Lion–winning opera Sun & Sea ; Emilija Škarnulytė , known for immersive films exploring ecology, mythology, and geopolitics; the Vilnius, Lithuania–based duo Pakui Hardware ; and Latvian-born sculptor Daiga Grantiņa . Her interest is not limited to artists who have already achieved institutional visibility. VV Foundation runs a prize for recent art-school graduates and supports exhibitions, publications, and residencies, creating an ecosystem around the collection rather than treating acquisition as its final purpose. At PAiR, the foundation’s residency in the coastal town of Pāvilosta, Latvia, artists are given time to develop new work in relative isolation. The program is based in a renovated 1901 house near the Baltic Sea. Artists who stay there may later enter the collection or receive support for exhibitions, though the relationships are not strictly transactional. The residency, collection, and foundation frequently overlap. The artist duo MAREUNROL’S stayed at PAiR while developing work for the Latvian Pavilion at the Venice Biennale , which VV Foundation has supported for four consecutive editions. Liberte still calls the foundation a hobby. “It’s something that we just love doing because we love artists,” she said. Yet her collecting has become part of a broader effort to establish a cultural record of a region whose artists have historically been overlooked internationally. For a lawyer accustomed to structures and regulations, she is drawn to art because it offers the opposite.“I’m also quite drawn to freedom,” she noted. “In art, you can say things, and you can experiment, and you can really break through things in your own way.” That freedom ultimately defines her collection: not a survey of what the Baltic art world is expected to be, but a record of artists insisting on their own ways of seeing.

title: Taryn Simon to debut new work for Guggenheim solo show in September 2026.
summary: The Guggenheim Museum in New York will dedicate its entire rotunda to a single artist working in photography and video for the first time when it opens “ Taryn Simon | Father Country I Do Love You” on September 18, 2026. Running through March 14, 2027, the exhibition will mark the first monographic rotunda presentation by a photography-based artist in the museum’s history as well as the largest debut of new work ever presented at the Guggenheim. Nearly a decade in the making, “Father Country I Do Love You” (2026) is Simon’s most expansive and personal project to date. Spread across 42 individual artworks combining photography, text, video, and sculpture, it traces the real life of an unnamed federal agent whose work as a middleman involved witnessing events and collecting evidence for others to piece together. But his work rippled outward into the lives of people and nations he never knew. The exhibition is dedicated to Simon’s father, who worked for the U.S. government in Thailand and traveled to Russia, Iran, Israel, China, Afghanistan, and Korea before embarking on a second career manufacturing and selling arcade games. Simon never learned his full story, and when he was diagnosed with Alzheimer's, it became impossible. Simon has spent two decades mining bureaucratic and institutional archives in her practice. These have ranged from the CIA’s art collection to the visa paperwork behind her 2016 Park Avenue Armory performance piece “ An Occupation of Loss ,” which grappled with loss in a spectacular set designed by OMA. Her 2024 sculpture Kleroterion at Storm King Art Center , meanwhile, modeled on an ancient Athenian voting device, grew in part from a childhood spent around her family’s arcade machines. “Games were like oxygen—always there,” said the artist, who has described her research process as inseparable from her medium. The works in “Father Country I Do Love You” will enter the Guggenheim’s permanent collection, which already holds three other pieces by Simon. The museum will also co-publish an accompanying artist book with Hatje Cantz. The exhibition is organized by curator Nat Trotman and was initiated by former artistic director Nancy Spector. Simon is represented by Gagosian and Almine Rech . Correction: An earlier version of this headline stated that Taryn Simon would be the first photography and film artist to have a solo show at the Guggenheim. The upcoming exhibition is the first by a lens-based artist to occupy the museum’s entire main space.

title: 5 Standout Shows to See at Small Galleries This August
summary: First Sun and Green Curtain, 2026 Shawn Huckins K Contemporary In this monthly roundup, we spotlight five stellar exhibitions at small and rising galleries. Alejandro Javaloyas “ Un cuchillo que no corta ” Galeria Reus , Palma, Spain Through Aug. 31 Tal vez los años luz son todos iguales, 2025 Alejandro Javaloyas Galeria Reus La pesanteur et la grâce, 2025 Alejandro Javaloyas Galeria Reus Spanish artist Alejandro Javaloyas presents new small and uncanny works based on his own recurring nightmares in this new exhibition , the title of which translates to “the knife that doesn’t cut.” For years, Javaloyas has diligently kept a record of his dreams in a notebook by his bedside. The artist takes these notes and works with artificial intelligence models to create visualizations of his scribblings. Pulling from hundreds of variations, Javaloyas selects a handful of images, which he then reworks digitally. These pictures are then printed as giclée prints on cotton paper, which the artist then layers with wax-based colored pencil that creates a kind of glaze. Picturing burning houses, crashed cars, and baby teeth, the works possess an ambiguous blur that gives the fleeting sensation of a dream. In one work, Tal vez los años luz son todos iguales (2025), a snail inches across the nape of the neck, to a surreal and visceral effect. The artist holds a master’s degree in film and the influence of filmmakers such as Andrei Tarkovsky, Chris Marker , and David Lynch is evident in his works’ atmospheric weight. Shawn Huckins “ Slow Burn ” K Contemporary , Denver Through Aug. 22 War Cloud and Floral Blue Curtain, 2026 Shawn Huckins K Contemporary Wildfire Sunrise Behind Floral Lace Curtain, 2026 Shawn Huckins K Contemporary Beyond the elegantly parted drapes, disaster awaits. Artist Shawn Huckins is known for his paintings which reimagine scenes from American art history, from the vast vistas painted by Albert Bierstadt (of the Hudson River School ) to the portraits of John Singleton Copley . These works delve into American national mythology and how it is remembered and rewritten. In his new show on view at Denver's K Contemporary , each painting is formatted like a window, with curtains painted parted to each side. While the curtains, which range from lace to a rich green satin, suggest well-appointed interiors, the world beyond the window is filled with war clouds and wildfires. These apocalyptic scenes are a new addition to Huckins’s precisely painted tableaux. The artist works from a studio in New Hampshire, and the recent series was partly inspired by the vibrant but hazy sunrises in the area caused by ongoing Canadian wildfire smoke. The hyperreal curtains suggest a kind of psychological distance from the unfolding disasters. The artist highlights the environmental effects of war and greater climate change on such majestic landscapes. Jordi Clotet Saló “ Primera pedra ” Alzueta Gallery , Barcelona Through Sep. 2 Accident, 2026 Jordi Clotet Saló Alzueta Gallery Jeroglífic, 2026 Jordi Clotet Saló Alzueta Gallery In this show, Catalan artist Jordi Clotet Saló presents a new series of oil-on-linen paintings with simplified forms. Painted in a limited palette of oxidized earth tones, these works range from geometric, almost architectural patterns, such as repeating circles broken into quadrants, and childlike depictions of cars and houses. The exhibition title “ Primera pedra ” translates as “first stone” and reflects his paradoxical feeling of always being at the beginning, starting from scratch. In Clotet’s case, this feeling is heightened when creating a new work, even as his imagery draws from a sense of nostalgia and memory. Clotet’s interest in origins factors into his material choices as well. The artist's pigments are extracted from a quarry in Zaragoza, Spain, and processed locally, giving these works a raw, natural feeling. “ Ripples of Light ” LA BIBI Gallery , online Through Oct. 31 Mallorca Shutter, 2025 Paul Riedmüller LA BIBI GALLERY Butterfly Sword Warrior, 2024 Fatima de Juan LA BIBI GALLERY What does summer feel like? “ Ripples of Light ,” an online presentation from LA BIBI Gallery , puts a spin on the traditional summer group show. Rather than actual depictions of the season (think beach scenes and bikinis), here, you’ll find works that embrace the sensory intensity of the hottest months. Across painting, sculpture, and mixed media, the works on view are marked by chromatic saturation, lush gesturalism, and a breezy, waterfront feel. Paul Riedmüller ’s Mallorca Shutter (2025), is a trompe l’oeil painting of closed bright green shutters, with stark shadowing under the slots. The painting calls to mind a blazing hot day, when the only respite is blocking out the sunlight. Elsewhere, abstractions evoke the sensations of the season through intensity of color. In Srger ’s acrylic, oil stick, and charcoal-on-wood composition BM_4 (2025), for example, a sweeping block of royal blue pigment dotted with bright white squiggles brings to mind a summer sky with crossing clouds. “ Summer Vibes - 2026 ” Daguet-Bresson , Ramatuelle, France Through Sept. 13 #2631, 2026 Morten Løbner Espersen Daguet Bresson Palengrotte, 2026 Superpoly Daguet Bresson Paris gallery Daguet-Bresson Gallery returns to the Saint-Tropez peninsula this summer with an exhibition at the Fondugues-Pradugues estate in Ramatuelle. The show, which brings together dozens of ceramic vessels, is full of whimsy and wonder, ranging from kaleidoscopic glazes to animalian tureens. Danish ceramist Morten Løbner Espersen 's vases are a standout of the show, as the seemingly simple vessels are transformed by thick layers of glazes. Also delightful are the quirky ceramics of French artist duo Superpoly (Antoine Grulier and Thomas Defour), including functional stoneware plates adorned with big-eyed fish and startled crabs.

title: Works by Goya, Caravaggio, and van Gogh appear in new trailer for “The Thomas Crown Affair,” starring Michael B. Jordan.
summary: The trailer for Amazon MGM Studios’s forthcoming remake of The Thomas Crown Affair was released this week—and a few art historical masterpieces make cameos. Directed by and starring Michael B. Jordan, the film, which is due in theaters March 5, 2027, tells the story of a high-end art thief. About 12 seconds into the trailer , Thomas Crown, played by Jordan, opens a hidden room behind sliding bookshelves to reveal a private stash of stolen paintings on a museum-style storage rack. ARTnews identified the four visible works, from left to right, as Francisco Goya ’s Saturn Devouring His Son (ca. 1820–23), which belongs to the Museo del Prado in Madrid; Henry Ossawa Tanner ’s The Banjo Lesson (1893), from the Hampton University Museum; Kerry James Marshall ’s Silence Is Golden (1986), from the Studio Museum in Harlem ; and Caravaggio ’s The Fortune Teller (ca. 1594), from Rome’s Capitoline Museums. Crown is shown holding a fifth canvas to add to the collection, and a little later in the trailer, he is seen attempting to steal a Vincent van Gogh “Sunflower” painting. The film also stars Adria Arjona as an insurance investigator tasked with catching Crown, and Kenneth Branagh as a rival he targets. Speaking to Variety , Jordan distanced the new film from its predecessors: “I didn’t want a reboot. I wanted a reimagination. The first two films were about rich white guys stealing for fun. That doesn’t land today. Ours is more personal. The stakes are higher. Still got the fashion, romance.” The original 1968 Thomas Crown Affair , starring American actor Steve McQueen, centered on a bank heist rather than art theft. The 1999 remake, with Pierce Brosnan in the lead, introduced the art-crime premise, with Crown stealing a Claude Monet painting of Venice’s San Giorgio Maggiore from the Metropolitan Museum of Art . As Artnet has reported , the film took liberties with the facts: the Met does not own that Monet, which exists in two versions housed in Wales and Japan, and the climactic “museum” scene was actually filmed at the New York Public Library rather than the Met itself. Jordan is no stranger to art-adjacent scenes on-screen. In Black Panther (2018), his character, Killmonger, confronts a curator inside a fictionalized British Museum stand-in before stealing a Wakandan artifact from a display case. Film heists involving real or invented artworks have a long pop-culture history. The 1962 James Bond film Dr. No , for instance, featured a reproduction of Goya’s Portrait of the Duke of Wellington —a painting that had, in fact, been stolen from the National Gallery , London, the year before and remained missing until 1965.

title: 5 Young London Collectors Pushing the Scene Forward
summary: What does it mean to collect art in London today? Perhaps the first problem with the question is the idea that there is a single London art world. Across the city, overlapping scenes operate at vastly different scales: artist-run spaces and young galleries sit alongside blue-chip dealers, auction houses, centuries-old collections, and some of the world’s most influential art schools. From Mayfair to Deptford, Fitzrovia to Bethnal Green, art is embedded across London, and there are as many ways into its art world as there are ways to participate in it. For collectors, this vastness creates an unusual proximity to artists and the communities around them. Someone might discover an artist at a graduate show or in a small gallery, follow their work across the city, and support their practice long before institutional or market recognition arrives. Artists, collectors, gallerists, students, curators, and dealers continually move between London’s different art worlds, creating relationships that connect its grassroots scenes to its established institutions and markets. London, 2011 Gilbert & George White Cube This also makes collecting in London amorphous. It can mean buying emerging artists from small galleries, pursuing historic objects through Mayfair dealerships and auction rooms, or simply purchasing a first work to live with at home. While the art market at large still contains its barriers, the sheer breadth of London’s scene offers multiple points of entry, across tastes, generations, communities, and budgets. Perhaps that plurality is what makes collecting in the Big Smoke so distinctive. There is no single route in, no single taste to follow, and no single definition of a collector. Artsy spoke to five collectors about how they navigate London’s overlapping art worlds, what drives them to buy, and the artists, galleries, and institutions that keep them excited about the city. Selim Bouafsoun collects with an international eye For Selim Bouafsoun, collecting is as much about relationships as it is about art. Though his relationship with art began from a young age, it was Alighiero Boetti ’s 2012 retrospective at Tate Modern that proved formative, opening up new ways of thinking about time, collaboration, and systems. Bouafsoun had always wanted to buy art, but initially found the prospect intimidating. Galleries, mentors, and friends eventually gave him the confidence to begin. “Collecting, I’ve come to realise, is never a solitary act,” he told Artsy. His first acquisition was a painting by Bernhard Buhmann , bought from Dubai gallery Carbon12 in November 2015. Today, his collection spans more than 100 artists, with recent acquisitions including Álvaro Barrington , Monia Ben Hamouda , Sebastián Espejo , and Tomasz Kowalski . One work remains particularly close to him: Hommage à Bonnard (1972) by the late Tunisian painter Hédi Turki . In London, Bouafsoun gravitates towards galleries willing to take risks, including Sadie Coles HQ, Carlos/Ishikawa, Emalin, and LBF Contemporary. But he sees some of the city’s greatest energy beyond its established art infrastructure, among artists and spaces operating with limited resources and ambitious ideas. He is particularly excited by an emerging generation shaped by international lives and communities. Their internationalism, he said, “isn’t performed; it’s lived.” Adelle Cohen believes collecting should be for everyone As a new collector, Adelle Cohen’s path into art began, unusually, with being told not to make any. At school, her art teacher would send her into town to buy supplies for the class rather than letting her participate. Her entry into collecting came years later at British artist Shauna Cribbin’s solo show at the Bomb Factory Art Foundation, where an iridescent screenprint on metal caught her attention. “I instantly fell in love and had to buy it,” Cohen recalled. “That’s how I became a collector.” Cohen’s London is centered on galleries in the city’s east, including Maureen Paley, Rose Easton, and Herald St, as well as Harlesden High Street in northwest London. She is drawn to programs that she sees as challenging without becoming exclusionary. That accessibility is central to how Cohen thinks about collecting. Rather than an activity reserved for an established collector class, she believes buying art should be an ordinary way of participating in London’s art scene. “Everyone should be encouraged to buy art,” she said. “We all deserve to own it.” Her taste isn’t entirely bound by seriousness either. The work she currently covets is by Dutch artist Diederik van Apple : an image of Nicolas Cage in the iconic film Leaving Las Vegas printed onto real dollar bills and submerged in glossy resin. “I shouldn’t love it,” Cohen admitted. “But I do.” Fabian Kluth collects through curiosity Fabian Kluth is reluctant to call himself a collector. “I see myself more as a project maker and entrepreneur,” he told Artsy. For him, art is an extension of a broader curiosity about people and what they choose to make. Kluth’s interest in contemporary art intensified during the COVID-19 lockdowns. While galleries and museums were closed, he was struck by how active the art world remained online. Social media became his way into a community he had previously observed from the outside. His first acquisition was a work on paper by German artist Rosa Loy . Since then, Kluth has gravitated towards artists with strong ideas who resist bending their practices to expectations. His collection includes Brett Charles Seiler , Pol Taburet , and Konrad Weichs. He is also drawn to women artists from older generations, including Nan Goldin and the late Swiss painter Irène Zurkinden . In London, Kluth is less interested in the set calendar of fairs and gallery weekends than in accidental discovery. He prefers wandering through the city and entering galleries without a plan, and points to Düsseldorf- and Berlin-based SETAREH ’s Mayfair space as a welcome recent addition. For Kluth, London’s strength lies in its mix of generations and international perspectives. Its art schools are central to that, with Central Saint Martins and the Slade School of Fine Art among the places he looks to for what might come next. Ultimately, his approach starts with people. “Whenever I meet someone,” Kluth said, “one of the first questions I ask is, ‘What are you currently working on?’” Daria Borisova backs artists early For London-based curator and art advisor Daria Borisova, collecting, curating, and community are closely connected. Her work has long centered on emerging artists, and that instinct for discovery carries into her collection: encountering an artist early, for her, is less about predicting the market than supporting a practice as it develops. One of Borisova’s earliest acquisitions was a painting by the late British artist Sarah Cunningham , whom she remembers for the sensitivity and personality of both her work and their interactions. Today, Borisova is drawn to artists developing distinctive ways of working. She points to The Artsy Vanguard alum Emily Kraus , who pulls canvases around constructed rooms to spread and smear paint across their surfaces; KV Duong , whose paintings on latex explore Vietnamese diasporic queer experience; and Antonio Társis , who transforms discarded matchboxes, cardboard, and paint tins into art. “These artists aren’t just making beautiful things,” Borisova said. “They’re making arguments.” Her collection also reflects an appetite for discovering artists early. George Rouy , Eva Helene Pade , Joseph Yaeger, Flora Yukhnovich , and Jadé Fadojutimi are among the artists she encountered before their wider recognition. For Borisova, this process of discovery is central to London’s appeal. Hayward Gallery and the Barbican Centre are favorite institutional haunts, but she sees the city’s real strength in the community around them: collectors, artists, and galleries invested in one another. “The energy starts here,” she said. “We find them first.” Linton Wang looks to the past for inspiration While many young collectors look for the next emerging artist, Linton Wang is more likely to be found pursuing an object several centuries old. His collecting began as a teenager with fountain pens, particularly examples from the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Their precious-metal decoration led him towards silver and decorative arts. Studies in history of art, followed by a master’s at the Courtauld Institute, expanded his interests across European art and material culture, with a particular focus on the Age of Enlightenment. For Wang, materiality is non-negotiable. Beauty of form, technical excellence, and fine materials take precedence over concept alone. He is fascinated by objects that have survived for centuries and the lives they have accumulated along the way. “Given one’s own brief existence, to imagine the lives of such works is itself an exercise of the mind,” he said. “Old works have the remarkable ability to grant access to people and ages that had long ceased to exist.” Perhaps unsurprisingly, his favorite London institution is the Wallace Collection, whose French Régence and Louis XV holdings align closely with his own tastes. “I have told myself that should I die without an heir, all my earthly possessions will go to that august institution,” he said. Wang also sees London’s historic art market as very much alive. He values the city’s auction houses for their breadth and accessibility, while its network of specialist dealers maintains a depth of expertise even as traditional dealerships become more private. One of his favorite acquisitions captures the thrill of that market. Wang first encountered an English Chinoiserie silver tea caddy from 1758 at an American auction in 2015, but lost it to another bidder. When it resurfaced a decade later, he bought it. The unknown collector who owned it in between had kept it in pristine condition. The two have never met, but for Wang, their connection through the object reflects the “unspoken camaraderie surrounding a thing of beauty” that makes collecting so compelling.

title: Kiaf SEOUL 2026 announces 175 exhibitors for its 25th edition.
summary: Kiaf SEOUL 2026, Korea’s largest contemporary art fair, has announced 175 exhibitors from 18 countries. Korea’s largest international art fair will return to COEX in Seoul from September 2–6, the same dates and location as Frieze Seoul. Organized by the Galleries Association of Korea, the fair marks its 25th anniversary and, for the first time, has appointed an external creative director: acclaimed designer Kuho Jung, known for his work across fashion, performance, and exhibition design. Jung who will lead the fair’s branding, spatial design, and special exhibition curation. The fair is a central pillar of Seoul Art Week, which connects exhibitions and programs across the city through major institutions including Leeum Museum of Art , Art Sonje Center and Space K. The week also includes district-based evening programs in the city’s gallery districts of Samcheong, Hannam, and Cheongdam. Kiaf SEOUL’s exhibitor list spans established and emerging galleries from Korea and internationally, including first-time participants Nino Mier Gallery and JD Malat Gallery . Returning exhibitors include Korean stalwarts such as Kukje Gallery , Gana Art , and Arario Gallery as well as major international names including Whitestone Gallery and Opera Gallery . The fair will present a mix of historically significant and contemporary works. Korean modern art is well represented, with pieces from Lee Ufan ’s “Wind” series, for example, shown across multiple galleries. Other Korean art highlights include mixed-media works by Dansaekhwa artist Seobo Park at Wellside Gallery, Nam June Paik ’s Internet Dweller wol.five.ydpb (1994) at CMay Gallery , and abstract works by Seund Ja Rhee at Galerie Vazieux. Other major 20th century works on view include a 1982 tempera by Marc Chagall at Art of the World Gallery, Sol LeWitt ’s Irregular Grid (1999) at Obscura Gallery , as well as works by Keith Haring at SH Gallery and David Hockney at Gallery Pici. Kiaf PLUS, the fair’s section for emerging and experimental practices, features eight Korean galleries alongside 11 international participants from Bangkok, Tokyo, New York, Moscow, Taipei, Madrid and Osaka. Kiaf HIGHLIGHTS, an initiative launched in 2023 to support participating artists, returns in an expanded format with dedicated in-booth exhibition spaces, with the aim of offering visitors a more focused viewing experience.
